Geopolitics.title: Who are the 'street medics' showing up at protests around the world?
Geopolitics.summary: From treating tear gas exposure to tending to injuries, street medics have become an increasingly common sight at protests all over the world. But who exactly are they and when did they start showing up at demonstrations? Story by Daniel Quinlan.

Geopolitics.title: Palestinian stories set for major presence at 2027 Oscars
Geopolitics.summary: Al Jazeera spoke to the director and cast of Who Is Still Alive, Switzerland’s Oscar entry for Best International Film.

Geopolitics.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
Geopolitics.summary: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.

Geopolitics.title: Ronaldo-less Portugal thrashed 4-1 by Denmark in the Nations League
Geopolitics.summary: Rasmus Hojlund stars with brace as Denmark close in on a spot in the Nations League quarterfinals.

Geopolitics.summary: With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down. Science.title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13) during the Starship Flight 15 test.

Science.title: SpaceX's Starship set for return to Earth after booster catch aborted
Science.summary: SpaceX said its Starship spacecraft was "healthy" as it orbited the Earth and on track to return Saturday to its Texas launch site, where Elon Musk's company was planning to "catch" the vehicle for the first time.

Science.title: SpaceX's Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
Science.summary: SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Science.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.

Science.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX's Starship megarocket reached orbit today (Nov. 13) during its 15th test flight, but the company scrapped a plan to catch the vehicle's massive booster back at the launch site.

Science.title: Measles is back in the United States, WHO authorities say
Science.summary: The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

Science.title: A newly discovered South African dinosaur was a heavyweight even as a youngster
Science.summary: It probably walked on two legs and weighed about 400 kilograms (880 pounds), despite still being a youngster. Meet Nyana rooiwalensis, a newly identified dinosaur species that lived more than 200 million years ago in what is now South Africa.

Science.title: California steels for storms that could trigger massive waves, flooding
Science.summary: California was bracing Friday for a storm series packing heavy rain and surf that could once again flood coastal communities and potentially send monster waves pounding shores.

Science.title: Archaeologists shed new light on wealth and status among Europe's early herders
Science.summary: How unequal were prehistoric societies? And how can archaeologists measure wealth in cultures that left behind no written records, no tax registers and no census data?

Science.title: Unstable plasma heats itself with waves it generates, experiments reveal
Science.summary: Fusion power is expected to be a sustainable energy source that emits no carbon dioxide during electricity generation. To achieve this, research is underway worldwide to confine high-temperature plasma using magnetic fields. To initiate a fusion reaction, high-energy particles or waves must be injected from outside to heat the plasma to extremely high temperatures.

Science.title: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
Science.summary: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.

Science.title: Does your culture shape how you look at art? What an eye‑tracking study in Sudan revealed
Science.summary: Today, Old Dongola is an abandoned settlement on the banks of the Nile in northern Sudan. Hundreds of years ago, however, this place looked very different.

Science.title: A common food emulsifier could solve one of rocketry's oldest fuel problems
Science.summary: In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids—in other words, they've been working with gels. Unfortunately, gels have their own sets of problems to deal with.

Science.title: The role of social relationships in scaling agricultural innovations: A dimension that remains underreported in research
Science.summary: A study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems reveals that, although partnerships and institutional collaboration feature prominently in climate-oriented agricultural research, their relationship with the scaling of innovations is rarely explicitly documented. The findings highlight the need to better understand the role of social relationships to strengthen the design, monitoring and evaluation of scaling processes.

Science.title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
Science.summary: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

Science.title: World's largest freshwater lake is recovering after decades of decline
Science.summary: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds around 20% of the world's surface freshwater, making it the most voluminous freshwater lake (Lake Superior on the United States–Canada border is the largest by surface area). This makes the lake one of the most important environments for biodiversity—in fact, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1996 because of this. Yet it has shown considerable decline over the last century, with aridification spreading across East Asia.

Science.title: Hidden 'master switch' allows bacteria to breach the body's defenses
Science.summary: Researchers at Penn Dental Medicine have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism by which bacteria rapidly compromise the body's protective barriers, a finding that could reshape how scientists approach a wide range of serious diseases.

Science.title: Heavier-than-expected electron behavior may explain slower electrical flow in alpha-gallium oxide
Science.summary: Power electronic devices help control the flow of electricity and convert it into forms needed by different machines, such as electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and industrial equipment. Some electrical energy is lost as heat during this process, reducing efficiency and potentially affecting the device's performance. Semiconductor materials that can withstand high voltages, carry electricity efficiently and release heat effectively would make these devices more efficient and reliable.

Science.title: Common ADHD classroom accommodations may not help students succeed, study finds
Science.summary: Extra time on assignments. Frequent breaks. A quiet place to work. For students with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), these are some of the most common accommodations schools provide to make learning easier. But are they actually helping children succeed? A new study from Florida International University (FIU) suggests that some widely used approaches may be falling short.

Science.title: Some of the oldest rocks ever discovered shed light on Earth's early history
Science.summary: Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old, according to estimates. However, rocks dating back to the planet's earliest days are extremely rare. Hence the excitement over the discovery in northern China of some of the oldest known rocks on Earth, dating back 3.95 billion years. And one of the reasons for all the attention is that they're revealing new clues about how Earth's crust formed and evolved.

Science.title: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
Science.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.

Science.title: Happy face, angry voice: Human–dog interaction study tracks conflicting cues
Science.summary: Dogs, having lived alongside humans for tens of thousands of years, are keenly tuned in to our emotions. Behavioral experiments, brain studies and even measurements of heart rate all suggest dogs respond differently depending on the emotional expressions they encounter in humans.

Science.title: Ancient rocks reveal a dramatic journey from deep inside Earth
Science.summary: Surface rocks can reveal records of regions they occupied millions of years ago, even if those areas were kilometers below ground. On Türkiye's Marmara Sea's southern shores and islands, granitic rocks that are now exposed originated as molten material deep in Earth's crust.

Science.title: A cosmic magnifying glass could reveal the same supernova two more times in roughly 70 years
Science.summary: Thanks to the gravitational lensing caused by a massive galaxy cluster and high-resolution images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers discovered an exploding star when the universe was 4.9 billion years old. The discovery paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 23, presents a prediction for when the rest of the distorted images of SN Ares will arrive.

Science.title: A dead star is flashing radio waves every 8 minutes, and its partner looks a lot like the sun
Science.summary: Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzling over a new kind of cosmic object called long-period radio transients. These are objects that emit bright flashes of radio waves into space every few minutes to every few hours. Some have been traced back to binary systems consisting of a small, dim, cool star called a red dwarf in orbit with a stellar remnant called a white dwarf.

Science.title: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (photos)
Science.summary: Rocket Lab launched its 100th space mission shortly after midnight on Saturday (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.

Science.title: Fiji petrel eludes 10-day search as communities aim to protect bird's habitat
Science.summary: A new study details scientists' search for one of the planet's rarest birds in the waters off Fiji's Gau Island. Spanning 10 days, the expedition yielded no verified sightings of the critically endangered Fiji petrel, one of the world's most elusive birds. Fewer than 50 individuals are believed to remain on Earth.

Science.title: Urban expansion causes ecological collapse in streams in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area
Science.summary: The advance of urbanization in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area in Brazil is causing the collapse of food webs in local streams. A study published in August in the journal Nature Cities reveals that the impact of the metropolis goes far beyond a simple reduction in species. Degradation selectively eliminates organisms based on their size and simplifies ecological interactions. Networks of 190 connections plummet to just three.

Science.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
Science.summary: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.

Science.title: 'Planimal' cells retain nearly entire algal genome after experimental cell fusion
Science.summary: Most DNA in an organism is inherited from its parent or parents. This form of genetic inheritance is referred to as vertical inheritance because genes are passed down from generation to generation.

Science.title: New genetic atlas reveals traces of 10,000 years of sheep breeding
Science.summary: For around 10,000 years, humans have selectively bred sheep for desirable traits. Generation after generation, we have chosen animals for their wool, size and reproductive characteristics and gradually left our mark on their DNA.

Science.title: 'Flames soon engulfed us': Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes his mission's riskiest moment
Science.summary: After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

Science.title: Modified $450 3D printer builds living materials with more than 100 layers
Science.summary: Living materials created with a 3D printer are like living tissues with one notable exception: You get to choose exactly which cells are in them, as well as their final 3D shape. Depending on the type of bacteria included in the print, the material can clean up contaminated water or break down waste materials such as plastic.

Science.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
Science.summary: We're scared of the Xenomorphs again, but Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 knows old-fashioned bug hunts shouldn't be a thing of the past.

Science.title: A perfect couple: Chromium keeps ruthenium grounded in water electrolysis
Science.summary: They say opposites attract, and many couples do fit this pattern. One is pragmatic and down-to-earth, while the other is a dreamer with their head in the clouds. Yet, these differences make them perfect for each other. According to researchers at ICFO, chemical interactions between atoms are not that different. Ruthenium, for instance, belongs to the "dreamer" class. It is commonly used in single-atom catalysts that speed up water electrolysis, which splits water to obtain green hydrogen. Science.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
Science.summary: The red planet Mars will shine a little over 1 degree from Jupiter on the night of Nov. 15-16.

Science.title: Molecular sensor makes invisible traces of mercury easier to see
Science.summary: Mercury contamination presents an obvious challenge: it is invisible. A glass of water or a piece of fruit can seem perfectly normal to the naked eye, even when trace amounts of toxic mercury are present. Detecting such minute levels usually requires specialized laboratory tools and trained experts.

Science.title: Alaska laments decline of its prized salmon populations
Science.summary: In his Alaskan community, fisherman Bob Candopoulos has long welcomed tourists to his business that's showcased by a sign featuring a king salmon.

Science.title: Genomic analysis restores species status to 12 overlooked Great Barrier Reef corals
Science.summary: An international team of scientists working with Queensland Museum's CoralBank project has uncovered previously hidden coral diversity on Australia's east coast, revealing that 12 corals once considered variations of other species are distinct species in their own right.

Science.title: A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet
Science.summary: Astronomers have uncovered a potentially enormous new dwarf planet beyond Pluto, hidden for years in one of the most crowded regions of the night sky. The discovery of 2026 ED138 could expand the solar system's official dwarf planet family and hints that more mysterious worlds may be lurking far beyond Neptune.

Science.title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
Science.summary: The California Science Center's brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center —the home of NASA's space shuttle Endeavour —officially opened to the public today (Nov. 13).

Science.title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
Science.summary: How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century

Science.title: Same farms, different answers: When nitrogen pollution estimates don't add up
Science.summary: To reduce nitrogen pollution stemming from synthetic fertilizer and livestock waste, California's Central Valley relies on five data sets to estimate surplus nitrogen. However, most parts of the United States use just one or two data sets—the U.S. Department of Agriculture's agricultural survey and census—to estimate nitrogen surplus.

Science.title: Fruit fly sleep protein yields peptides that inhibit drug-resistant bacteria in lab tests
Science.summary: Researchers at University of Tsukuba and collaborating institutions have identified short antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri, a sleep-inducing protein in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

Science.title: 'Links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial': How DNA solved the 70-year mystery of what happened to the executed members of the last Russian imperial family
Science.summary: In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

Science.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
Science.summary: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?

Science.title: Which animal farts the most?
Science.summary: Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.
